seo.description: Moses in plain words: the burning bush, the plagues and the sea, Sinai and the Ten Commandments, his death on Mount Nebo, his feast days, and the myths.

who: Moses was a Hebrew born in Egypt and raised in Pharaoh's household. God called him from a burning bush to bring Israel out of slavery. He led them through the sea and the desert for forty years. On Mount Sinai he received the Ten Commandments. He died within sight of the promised land.

tidbits.text: Josephus says the name is Egyptian: “the Egyptians call water by the name of Mo, and such as are saved out of it, by the name of Uses”. *Britannica* hears *mose*, “is born”, as in Thutmose.
Numbers calls him “a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth.”
King Hezekiah broke up the bronze snake Moses made, “for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it.” They called it Nehushtan.
Justin Martyr, about 155, argued that Plato had learned from Moses, “the first prophet, and of greater antiquity than the Greek writers”.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In **Egypt**, to Amram and Jochebed, of the tribe of **Levi**. The year is argued over. Read literally, 1 Kings 6:1 puts the Exodus about **1440 BC**. *Britannica* prefers about **1290 BC**, under Ramses II.

facts.label: Raised
facts.text: In **Pharaoh's household**, as the son of Pharaoh's daughter. Stephen says he was “educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians”.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His brother **Aaron** was three years older. His sister was **Miriam**. He married **Zipporah**, a daughter of the priest of Midian, and they had two sons, **Gershom** and **Eliezer**. Numbers also speaks of a Cushite wife.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **shepherd** in Midian, keeping his father-in-law's flock. Then the **leader of Israel** for forty years.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Moshe**, in Hebrew. **The man of God**, in Deuteronomy and Psalm 90. **The servant of the LORD**, at his death. **The God-seer**, in the Orthodox Church. **The lawgiver**, in the *Roman Martyrology*.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: On **Mount Nebo**, in Moab, at **120**, within sight of the promised land.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: By God Himself, “in a valley in the land of Moab facing Beth-peor”. And “no one to this day knows the location of his grave.”

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Jewish and Christian tradition gives him the first five books of the Bible, the **Torah**. Jesus called it “the Book of Moses”. **Psalm 90** is headed with his name. Thomas Hobbes doubted he wrote it all in 1651, and many scholars have since. See Often misquoted.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Holding the **two tablets** of the Law. Often with **rays** of light from his head, or **horns**, from a word in the Latin Bible (see Often misquoted).

portrait.alt: An icon on a gold ground: a young, beardless Moses in a pale blue tunic and a red cloak bends down to untie his sandal. His other sandal lies on the ground behind him. On the right, a bush burns with red flame among brown rocks.

quotes.q: He was one that exceeded all men that ever were in understanding, and made the best use of what that understanding suggested to him.

moments.title: The basket in the reeds
moments.text: Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile. A Levite woman hid her son for three months. When she could hide him no longer, she coated a papyrus basket with tar and pitch and set it among the reeds by the river. His sister watched from a distance. Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe and found the boy crying, and she had compassion on him. His sister offered to fetch a Hebrew nurse, and brought his own mother. When he was older, Pharaoh's daughter took him as her son. She named him Moses: “I drew him out of the water.”

moments.title: A killing, and a flight
moments.text: When Moses was forty, says Stephen, he went out to see his own people at their hard labour. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. He looked this way and that, struck the Egyptian down, and hid his body in the sand. The next day two Hebrews were fighting, and one threw it back at him: “Who made you ruler and judge over us?” Pharaoh sought to kill him, and Moses fled to Midian. At a well there, shepherds drove seven sisters away from the troughs. Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock. Their father gave him one of them, Zipporah, as his wife. He named his first son Gershom: “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land.”

moments.title: The burning bush
moments.text: Moses was keeping his father-in-law's flock when he came to Horeb. There a bush was ablaze with fire, “but it was not consumed.” When he went over to look, God called to him from the bush: “Moses, Moses!” He answered, “Here I am.” “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God. God said He had seen the affliction of His people, and He was sending Moses to Pharaoh. Moses asked, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?” And what should he tell them if they asked God's name? “I AM WHO I AM.”

moments.title: “Send someone else”
moments.text: Moses had more objections. What if the people would not believe him? God gave him signs: his staff became a snake, and his hand turned leprous and was healed. Then Moses tried again. “I have never been eloquent, neither in the past nor since You have spoken to Your servant, for I am slow of speech and tongue.” God answered, “Who gave man his mouth?” and “Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” But Moses replied, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” The LORD's anger burned against him. Yet He gave him his brother Aaron, who could speak well, to be his spokesman.

moments.title: “Let My people go”
moments.text: Moses was eighty, and Aaron eighty-three, when they stood before Pharaoh. “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.’” Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” He made the Hebrews gather their own straw, for the same quota of bricks. The foremen turned on Moses, and Moses turned to God: “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?”

moments.title: The Passover
moments.text: After nine plagues, God sent a tenth. Each Israelite household killed a lamb and put its blood on the doorframes. At midnight the firstborn of Egypt died, from Pharaoh's son to the prisoner's, “for there was no house without someone dead.” Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron by night: “Get up, leave my people, both you and the Israelites!” About 600,000 men on foot went out, with women and children, after 430 years in Egypt. Moses took the bones of Joseph with them.

moments.title: Hands held up
moments.text: The Amalekites attacked Israel at Rephidim. Joshua led the fighting, while Moses stood on a hilltop with the staff of God. “As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed.” When his hands grew heavy, Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held his hands up, one on each side, until the sun went down. Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner.

moments.title: Advice from his father-in-law
moments.text: Moses sat as judge for the people from morning until evening. His father-in-law Jethro watched, and said, “What you are doing is not good. Surely you and these people with you will wear yourselves out, because the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone.” Choose capable, God-fearing men, he said, and set them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them judge the small cases, and bring only the hard ones to you. “Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said.”

moments.title: The mountain of fire
moments.text: In the third month out of Egypt, Israel camped at Sinai. On the third day there was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud, and a loud blast of the ram's horn. “Mount Sinai was completely enveloped in smoke, because the LORD had descended on it in fire.” God spoke the Ten Commandments. The people trembled and begged Moses, “Speak to us yourself and we will listen.” Later Moses entered the cloud on the mountain, and stayed there forty days and forty nights. There God gave him the two tablets of stone. How the ten are counted is under The Ten Commandments, below.

moments.title: The golden calf
moments.text: Moses was gone so long that the people gave up on him. “As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!” Aaron melted their gold earrings into a calf. On the mountain, God told Moses to leave Him alone, so that He could destroy them and make a great nation from Moses instead. Moses pleaded for them, and the LORD relented. Then Moses came down with the tablets. When he saw the calf and the dancing, he threw them down and shattered them. He burned the calf, ground it to powder, and made the people drink it. The next day he went back up to God, to ask forgiveness for them, or else to be blotted out with them.

moments.title: “Show me Your glory”
moments.text: Moses used to pitch a tent outside the camp, and the pillar of cloud would come down at its entrance. “Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.” Once he asked for more: “Please show me Your glory.” God said, “You cannot see My face, for no one can see Me and live.” On the mountain He would set Moses in a cleft of the rock, and cover him with His hand as His glory passed. Then Moses would see His back. So the LORD passed by, calling out, “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness”.

moments.title: The shining face
moments.text: Moses cut two new tablets and went up again for forty days and nights. When he came down, “he was unaware that his face had become radiant from speaking with the LORD.” Aaron and the people were afraid to come near him. So after he spoke to them, he covered his face with a veil. He took it off whenever he went in to speak with the LORD. Paul later took the veil as a picture: “whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.”

moments.title: “I cannot carry all these people”
moments.text: The people wept for meat. “We remember the fish we ate freely in Egypt, along with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic.” Moses had had enough. “I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me.” If this was how it would be, he asked God to kill him now. God told him to gather seventy elders, and put some of the Spirit that was on Moses on them. Two of the seventy, Eldad and Medad, prophesied in the camp instead of at the tent. Joshua wanted them stopped. Moses would not stop them.

moments.when: At the edge of the land
moments.title: Twelve spies
moments.text: Moses sent twelve men to spy out Canaan. After forty days they came back with grapes, pomegranates and figs, and with fear. The people there were giants, they said: “We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight.” Only Caleb and Joshua disagreed: “The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land.” The people wept all night, talked of choosing a leader to take them back to Egypt, and threatened to stone Joshua and Caleb. Moses pleaded for them again, and God pardoned them. But that generation would not enter the land. Israel would wander forty years, “a year for each day”.

moments.title: The rock at Meribah
moments.text: At Kadesh his sister Miriam died, and again there was no water. God told Moses and Aaron to take the staff and speak to the rock in front of the people. Instead Moses said, “Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?” and struck the rock twice with his staff. Water gushed out. But God said, “Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.”

moments.title: With Jesus, transfigured
moments.text: The Gospels bring Moses back once more. Jesus took Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray. His face changed, and His clothes became radiantly white. “Suddenly two men, Moses and Elijah, began talking with Jesus.” Luke says they “spoke about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word for departure is *exodos*. Peter offered to put up three shelters, one of them for Moses. Then a voice came from a cloud: “This is My Son, Whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!”

cite.text: Luke 9:28-36; Matthew 17:1-8; Strong's Greek 1841, at Bible Hub

miracles.lede: Exodus and Numbers tell of signs and wonders in Egypt and in the desert. Moses said plainly whose doing they were:

pledge.q: This is how you will know that the LORD has sent me to do all these things, for it was not my own doing

items.title: Water to blood
items.text: Moses and Aaron went to meet Pharaoh at the river. In front of him and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile.
items.quote: and all the water was turned to blood
items.witness: The fish died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink from it.

items.title: Gnats
items.text: Pharaoh's magicians had copied the first signs by their magic arts. Then Aaron struck the dust with his staff, and it turned into gnats on man and beast. The magicians tried to do the same, and could not.
items.quote: This is the finger of God
items.witness: So the magicians told Pharaoh. But his heart was hardened, and he would not listen.

items.title: Darkness you could touch
items.text: Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and a “palpable darkness” covered the land of Egypt for three days. No one could see anyone else, and no one left his place.
items.quote: Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings.

note.text: The ten, in order: the Nile turned to blood, frogs, gnats, flies, the death of the livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, and the death of the firstborn. The last is told in his life, above.

more.title: The sea divided
more.text: Pharaoh's army trapped Israel against the sea. Moses stretched out his hand over it, “and all that night the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind that turned it into dry land.” When the Egyptians followed, the waters flowed back over them. Then Moses and Miriam led the people in song.
more.quote: the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left.

more.title: Bread from heaven
more.text: In the desert the people grumbled that they would starve. God said, “I will rain down bread from heaven for you.” Each morning thin flakes lay on the ground. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. They called it manna, and ate it for forty years.
more.quote: It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.

more.title: Water from the rock
more.text: At Rephidim there was no water, and the people were ready to stone him. God told him to strike the rock at Horeb with his staff, and water came out for the people to drink. Moses named the place Massah and Meribah, because they quarrelled and tested the LORD. Years later, at Kadesh, water came from a rock again, and that time it cost him the land.
more.quote: Is the LORD among us or not?

more.title: The bronze snake
more.text: Venomous snakes bit the people, and many died. God told Moses to make a serpent and set it on a pole. Jesus later said, “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up”.
more.quote: If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live.

more.title: The ground opens
more.text: His cousin Korah and 250 leaders rose against him. Moses said that if these men died a natural death, the LORD had not sent him. “As soon as Moses had finished saying all this, the ground beneath them split open”.
more.quote: the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them and their households

doubt.title: Josephus left it to his readers
doubt.text: Josephus retold the crossing of the sea about 93, for readers across the Roman world. He wrote it down “as I found it in the sacred books”, and set beside it a story they knew: the Pamphylian Sea had drawn back for Alexander the Great. Then he let each reader decide: “as to these events, let every one determine as he pleases.”

words.note: Tradition gives Moses the first five books of the Bible, and Psalm 90 is headed with his name. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.q: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength.
feature.ctx: Moses taught it to Israel before they crossed the Jordan. When a scribe asked Jesus, “Which commandment is the most important of all?”, He answered with these words.

quotes.q: Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD's salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.
quotes.who: To the people, trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea.

quotes.q: Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin.... But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written.
quotes.who: To God, the day after the golden calf.

quotes.q: Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!
quotes.who: To Joshua, who wanted two men stopped from prophesying in the camp.

quotes.q: man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
quotes.who: On the manna. Jesus answered the devil with these words in the wilderness.

quotes.q: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live
quotes.who: His last charge to Israel, on the plains of Moab.

quotes.q: Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid or terrified of them, for it is the LORD your God Who goes with you; He will never leave you nor forsake you.
quotes.who: To all Israel, before they crossed the Jordan without him.

quotes.q: So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.
quotes.who: From Psalm 90, headed “A prayer of Moses the man of God”.

extras.title: The Ten Commandments
extras.lede: On Sinai, God gave Moses two tablets of stone, “inscribed by the finger of God”. Exodus calls their words “the Ten Commandments”, but it never numbers them, or says how they were shared between the two tablets. Josephus has “five upon each table”. So Jews and Christians count the ten in different ways. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: The Jewish count
items.text: In Jewish tradition the first of the Ten Words is not a command at all. It is God's own introduction, at the head of the ten. No other gods and no idols together make the second word, says the *Jewish Encyclopedia*. The command not to covet, all of it, is the tenth.
items.quote: I am the LORD your God, Who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

items.title: Catholic and Lutheran
items.text: In the 400s Augustine made no other gods and no idols a single commandment. To keep the number ten, he split the last in two: not coveting a neighbour's wife, and not coveting his goods. The Council of Trent kept his count, and so did the Lutherans. In Luther's *Small Catechism* the second commandment is “Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain.” The *Catholic Encyclopedia* explains why idols are not counted apart:
items.quote: the reference to idols being regarded as mere application of the precept to adore but one God

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, “Commandments of God”; Luther, Small Catechism, in Schaff's The Creeds of Christendom

items.title: Orthodox
items.text: The Orthodox count as Philo and Josephus did: no idols is the second commandment on its own, and coveting is one. Josephus put it plainly: “The second commands us not to make the image of any living creature to worship it.” The Orthodox *Longer Catechism* then asks whether icons break it. Its answer:
items.quote: it is not in the least contrary to this commandment to honor icons as sacred representations

cite.text: Josephus, Antiquities, book 3, chapter 5; the Longer Catechism, question 521, tr. R. W. Blackmore

items.title: Reformed and Anglican
items.text: The churches of England and Switzerland count the same way, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*, following Philo, Josephus and Origen. But the Reformed read the second commandment more strictly. The *Westminster Shorter Catechism* of 1647 teaches:
items.quote: The second commandment forbiddeth the worshiping of God by images, or any other way not appointed in His Word.

cite.text: Westminster Shorter Catechism, question 51, in Schaff's The Creeds of Christendom; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Commandments of God”

myths.truth: Exodus says that when he came down from Sinai, “his face was radiant”. The Hebrew verb, *qaran*, comes from the word for a horn, and means to send out rays. Jerome's Latin Bible put it as {la|cornuta esset facies sua}: his face was horned. The Douay-Rheims Bible kept the word: “he knew not that his face was horned from the conversation of the Lord.” Its own note explains, “That is, shining, and sending forth rays of light like horns.” Artists took the word as it stood. Michelangelo's marble Moses, carved about 1513 for the tomb of Pope Julius II, has two horns.

cite.text: Exodus 34:29-30; Strong's Hebrew 7160, at Bible Hub; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims, Exodus 34; Britannica

myths.truth: The Bible never says so. He said he was “slow of speech and tongue”, and did not say why. Stephen calls him “powerful in speech and action”. Josephus says “He had a very graceful way of speaking and addressing himself to the multitude”. The stutter comes from a later Jewish legend, told in the Midrash. As a small child, it says, Moses was tested with a precious stone and a live coal, and an angel guided his hand to the coal. The *Jewish Encyclopedia* of 1906 tells how it ends: “This burned his tongue, causing him to stutter”.

cite.text: Exodus 4:10; Acts 7:22; Josephus, Antiquities, book 4, chapter 8; Jewish Encyclopedia, “Moses”

myths.truth: The Hebrew name is Yam Suph. Suph means reeds: it is the word for the reeds where his basket was set. *Britannica* reads it as the Sea of Reeds, “most probably a shallow lake in the far northeastern corner of Egypt”, and calls the Red Sea an “erroneous interpretation”. Others keep the Red Sea. The New Testament, written in Greek, calls it the Red Sea. The same Hebrew name is used for the gulf at Eloth, which is an arm of the Red Sea. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1911 has him cross the Red Sea “at a point today unknown”. Exodus itself says it was the LORD Who drove the sea back, “with a strong east wind”.

cite.text: Exodus 2:3; 14:21; Acts 7:36; Hebrews 11:29; 1 Kings 9:26; Strong's Hebrew 5488, at Bible Hub; Britannica; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Moses”

myths.claim: Moses wrote the account of his own death.
myths.truth: Deuteronomy ends with his death and burial. Who wrote that page has been asked for two thousand years. Philo, a Jewish writer of Jesus' day, says Moses foresaw it: “he prophesied admirably what should happen to himself after his death”. The Talmud records two views. One asks, “Is it possible that Moses himself should have written ‘and he died’?”, and gives the last eight verses to Joshua. The other says God dictated them, “and Moses with tears in his eyes wrote it down.” In 1651 Thomas Hobbes took the line about the unknown grave as proof of a later hand: “it were a strange interpretation, to say Moses spake of his own sepulcher (though by Prophecy), that it was not found to that day, wherein he was yet living.”

cite.text: Deuteronomy 34:5-12; Philo, On the Life of Moses, book 2, tr. C. D. Yonge; the Talmud, Baba Bathra, chapter 1, tr. Michael L. Rodkinson; Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, chapter 33

circle.name: Elijah
circle.text: The prophet who, centuries later, walked forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, where Moses had met God. At the Transfiguration the two appeared together, talking with Jesus.

circle.name: Aaron
circle.text: His brother, three years older, and his spokesman before Pharaoh. While Moses was on the mountain, Aaron made the golden calf. His excuse: “when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!” He became the first high priest, and died on Mount Hor.

circle.name: Miriam
circle.text: His sister. After the sea she led the women with a tambourine. Later she and Aaron spoke against him, and she became leprous. Moses cried out, “O God, please heal her!” She died at Kadesh.

circle.name: Jethro
circle.text: His father-in-law, the priest of Midian, also called Reuel. He watched Moses judge the people alone from morning till evening and told him, “What you are doing is not good.”

circle.name: Zipporah
circle.text: His wife, a daughter of the priest of Midian, whom he met at a well. She bore him two sons, Gershom and Eliezer.

circle.name: Joshua
circle.text: His young assistant, who went up the mountain with him and would not leave the tent. Moses renamed him: Hoshea became Joshua. Moses laid his hands on him, and he led Israel into the land.

circle.name: Pharaoh's daughter
circle.text: She found him crying in a basket among the reeds and had compassion on him. She paid his own mother to nurse him, raised him as her son, and named him. Josephus calls her Thermuthis.

circle.name: Pharaoh
circle.text: The king who would not let Israel go. “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?” he asked. After the tenth plague he summoned Moses by night: “Get up, leave my people”. The Bible never gives his name.

circle.name: Korah
circle.text: His cousin, a Levite, who led 250 leaders against him: “You have taken too much upon yourselves!” The ground split open beneath the rebels.

death.big: He died on Mount Nebo, in Moab, at 120. From the top God showed him the whole promised land, but he never crossed into it.
paras: He begged to go in. “Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan.” The answer was no. “That is enough,” the LORD said. “Do not speak to Me again about this matter.” The reason went back to the rock at Meribah.

He laid his hands on Joshua and blessed the tribes. Then he climbed Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, facing Jericho. The LORD showed him the land, from Gilead as far as Dan and the Negev, and said, “I have let you see it with your own eyes, but you will not cross into it.”

“So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, as the LORD had said.” God Himself buried him, in a valley facing Beth-peor, “and no one to this day knows the location of his grave.” He was 120, and “his eyes were not weak”. Israel wept for him thirty days. The Coptic synaxarium gives a reason for the hidden grave: God hid his body “so the children of Israel would not find it and worship it”.

The Letter of Jude remembers a quarrel over his body. The archangel Michael “disputed with the devil over the body of Moses”, and said only, “The Lord rebuke you!” Origen says Jude took this from a book called *The Ascension of Moses*, “a little treatise, of which the Apostle Jude makes mention in his Epistle”.

later.title: The story Josephus told
later.text: Josephus, writing about 93, says Moses did not simply die. As he said goodbye to Eleazar and Joshua, “a cloud stood over him on the sudden, and he disappeared in a certain valley”. Why then does Scripture say he died? Moses wrote it himself, says Josephus, “out of fear, lest they should venture to say that, because of his extraordinary virtue, he went to God.”

cite.text: Josephus, Antiquities, book 4, chapter 8, tr. William Whiston

saint.big: Yes, as a prophet. He is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic calendars, on 4 September.

churches.note: Not in the English or Episcopal calendars

paras: The Orthodox call him the God-seer. On Sinai he saw God's glory pass by, and on another mountain he stood with the transfigured Christ. The OCA tells a later story from Sinai. When John of the Ladder became abbot there, a stranger was seen giving orders to the cooks. John said it was Moses: “Our lord Moses does nothing strange by serving in the place which belongs to him.”

Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, opens 4 September with “the holy lawgiver and prophet Moses”, on Mount Nebo in the land of Moab. There is no Mass for him in the Roman calendar, but the Litany of the Saints, in the form Rome published in 1969, calls on him by name among the patriarchs and prophets.
The Missouri Synod's calendar remembers him on the same day, as the lawgiver and prophet to whom the first five books of the Bible are attributed.

kin.name: Gideon
kin.text: When the angel called him, he answered, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father's house.” He asked for signs before he went. Then God sent him against Midian with three hundred men.

kin.name: Martha
kin.text: Busy with all the preparations while Jesus taught, she asked Him to tell her sister to help. “You are worried and upset about many things,” He said. When her brother died, she was the one who went out to meet Him.
